examples.title: Reuse a finished request key
examples.summary: Key 11 is already remembered as voided for 300¢. The same key requests 300¢ again.
examples.expected_output: Return duplicate, leave the entire state unchanged and request no effects. Key 11 remains voided and the used totals stay zero.
examples.challenge: The deliberate source patch treats a declined or voided key as fresh, so this request can append another entry for key 11.
examples.lesson: Available capacity does not make an old identity new. Released keys must remain remembered.

examples.title: Free counters after a timeout
examples.summary: Hold 11 was sent for 300¢ and still uses one slot. Its authorization reply times out.
examples.expected_output: Change hold 11 to unknown while retaining 300¢ and one slot. Return marked_unknown and no effects.
examples.challenge: The deliberate patch keeps the unknown entry but subtracts its 300¢ and slot, leaving both used counters at zero.
examples.lesson: The entry and counters must agree. P06 presents this same kind of proposed output; P03 instead invents a terminal decline.

examples.title: Retry under a different key
examples.summary: Hold 11 is unknown for 300¢. Retry its authorization using the stored identity and amount.
examples.expected_output: Change hold 11 to sent, retain 300¢ and one slot, return retried and request {:authorize, 11, 300}.
examples.challenge: The deliberate patch requests authorization for key 12 instead, while the ledger entry still belongs to key 11.
examples.lesson: Retrying the same hold must preserve its remote identity. Correct local counters do not establish that the requested effect names the right key.

examples.title: Refuse an exact-fit request
examples.summary: An empty account has a 100¢ limit and one slot. Fresh key 11 requests exactly 100¢.
examples.expected_output: Reserve 100¢ and one slot for key 11, record reserved status, return admitted and request no effects.
examples.challenge: The deliberate patch changes the amount rejection test from > to >=, so equality is refused as insufficient_amount.
examples.lesson: A rejected exact-fit request leaves a valid empty ledger but violates required admission.

examples.title: Refuse every eligible request
examples.summary: An empty account has 1000¢ of capacity and three slots. Fresh key 22 requests only 100¢.
examples.expected_output: Add key 22 as a reserved 100¢ hold, set used totals to 100¢ and one slot, return admitted and request no effects.
examples.challenge: The deliberate patch replaces the successful admission branch with insufficient_amount and an unchanged state.
examples.lesson: Refusing every request can preserve all upper bounds. A separate admission claim requires useful service for eligible inputs.

examples.title: Treat acknowledgment as approval
examples.summary: Hold 11 is sent for 300¢. A transport acknowledgment arrives without an approval result.
examples.expected_output: Leave the entire state unchanged, return stale and request no effects. Hold 11 remains sent with 300¢ and one slot held.
examples.challenge: The deliberate patch changes the sent entry to authorized and returns authorized when it receives only the acknowledgment.
examples.lesson: Delivery acknowledgment supplies no processor approval. Sent and authorized use the same capacity, so accounting alone misses this error.

examples.title: Forget the cancellation request
examples.summary: Hold 11 is authorized for 300¢. Ask to cancel it at the processor.
examples.expected_output: Set hold 11 to voiding, retain 300¢ and one slot, return voiding and request {:void, 11}.
examples.challenge: The deliberate patch keeps the expected state and result but removes the required void effect.
examples.lesson: Retaining capacity addresses exposure while the effect requests the unfinished cancellation. P02 isolates the missing-effect error.

examples.title: Increase used amount on decline
examples.summary: Hold 11 is sent for 300¢ and occupies one slot. Its processor result is declined.
examples.expected_output: Keep key 11 and its 300¢ amount with declined status, reduce both used counters to zero, return declined and request no effects.
examples.challenge: The deliberate patch adds 300¢ instead of subtracting it. Used amount becomes 600¢ even though the declined entry holds no capacity.
examples.lesson: A correct terminal label does not repair incorrect counters. The next-state validity claim checks their agreement.

examples.title: Keep sent status after restart
examples.summary: Hold 11 was sent for 300¢ before the process restarted. No terminal outcome is available.
examples.expected_output: Change hold 11 from sent to unknown, retain 300¢ and one slot, return restarted and request no effects.
examples.challenge: The deliberate patch leaves the entry sent instead of recording the uncertainty introduced by restart.
examples.lesson: Both statuses use the same capacity, so this fault can pass a validity-only restart check. The restart claim also requires that no sent entries remain.

examples.title: Release before cancellation is confirmed
examples.summary: Hold 1 is authorized for the account’s full 100¢. Request cancellation, then try another 100¢ request under key 2.
examples.expected_output: Set hold 1 to voiding, retain 100¢ and one slot, return voiding and request {:void, 1}. A following {:request, 2, 100} must return insufficient_amount.
examples.challenge: The deliberate patch returns voided and frees both counters while still requesting the remote void. The old authorization may remain live.
examples.lesson: Requesting cancellation does not establish completion. P05 presents this patch-shaped proposal; P01 also omits the effect.

examples.title: Cancel an approved hold too early
examples.summary: Hold 1 is authorized for 100¢, using all the amount capacity. Request its cancellation.
examples.expected_output: Keep 100¢ and one slot held, change hold 1 to voiding, return voiding and request {:void, 1}.
examples.challenge: The proposed output marks hold 1 voided, frees both counters, returns voided and requests no remote work.
examples.lesson: The proposal has two defects: premature release and missing work. Its supplied voided result lets both validity and the effects predicate accept the proposal; retention rejects it.

examples.title: Keep capacity, omit cancellation work
examples.summary: Hold 1 is authorized for 100¢. Request cancellation while its processor authorization may still be live.
examples.expected_output: Set hold 1 to voiding, retain 100¢ and one slot, return voiding and request {:void, 1}.
examples.challenge: The proposed output retains the right hold and counters but supplies an empty effects list.
examples.lesson: This proposal isolates the missing effect. Validity and retention permit it, while the effects predicate requires the void request. Emitting that request would still not prove delivery.

examples.title: Invent a decline after silence
examples.summary: Hold 1 was sent for 100¢. Its reply times out before the ledger receives a trusted result.
examples.expected_output: Change hold 1 to unknown, retain 100¢ and one slot, return marked_unknown and request no effects.
examples.challenge: The proposed output marks the hold declined, frees both counters and returns declined.
examples.lesson: A timeout establishes uncertainty. An invented terminal status can have internally consistent counters while violating retention. A second request could use capacity still held remotely.

examples.title: Refuse a request that fits exactly
examples.summary: An empty account has a 100¢ limit and one slot. Fresh key 11 requests exactly 100¢.
examples.expected_output: Add a reserved 100¢ entry for key 11, use 100¢ and one slot, return admitted and request no effects.
examples.challenge: The proposed output returns insufficient_amount and leaves the account empty.
examples.lesson: Keeping a valid state is insufficient when the requirement says an eligible request must be accepted.

examples.title: Send the void, release too early
examples.summary: Hold 1 is authorized for 100¢. Its cancellation has been requested, but no confirmation has arrived.
examples.expected_output: Keep hold 1 voiding with 100¢ and one slot held, return voiding and request {:void, 1}.
examples.challenge: The proposed output supplies the void effect but marks the hold voided and immediately frees both counters.
examples.lesson: This proposal matches the shape of the M10 source fault. A requested effect does not establish completion. Both retention and effects consistency reject it.

examples.title: Keep the unknown label, free its counters
examples.summary: Hold 1 is sent for 100¢ and one slot. Process a timeout for that hold.
examples.expected_output: Keep 100¢ and one slot counted, change the entry to unknown, return marked_unknown and request no effects.
examples.challenge: The proposed output keeps the unknown entry but sets both used counters to zero.
examples.lesson: The retention predicate accepts the same key and amount in unknown status; validity rejects the counters. This is the shape of the M2 fault, not P03’s invented decline.

examples.title: Change an unrelated hold
examples.summary: Hold 1 is authorized for 50¢ and hold 2 is sent for 100¢. Their account permits 250¢ and three slots. Only hold 2 times out.
examples.expected_output: Keep hold 1 authorized, change hold 2 to unknown, retain totals of 150¢ and two slots, return marked_unknown and request no effects.
examples.challenge: The proposed output also marks hold 1 voided and reduces the totals to 100¢ and one slot.
examples.lesson: The proposal has consistent totals and preserves both keys and amounts. Check retention for protected key 1 even though the event targets key 2.

examples.title: Cancel before dispatch
examples.summary: Hold 1 reserves 100¢ locally and has never been dispatched. Request its cancellation.
examples.expected_output: Mark hold 1 voided, release 100¢ and one slot, return voided and request no remote work. Keep key 1 and its original amount remembered.
examples.challenge: The proposed output does exactly this. It is the correct local-cancellation control case.
examples.lesson: A rule that always waits for remote confirmation would wrongly reject this local cancellation. A fresh request under key 2 can now fit; the post-dispatch retention precondition does not apply.
